content: 1. The recommended potassium intake for adults and children aged 2 years and older is outlined in specific guidelines to ensure proper health and nutrition. 2. WHO provides guidance on ending the inappropriate promotion of foods targeted at infants and young children, emphasizing the importance of ethical marketing practices. 3. The WHO Global Report on Sodium Intake Reduction highlights strategies to lower sodium consumption worldwide, aiming to reduce the risk of hypertension and related diseases. 4. WHO has developed a manual on sugar-sweetened beverage taxation policies to promote healthier diets and reduce the consumption of sugary drinks. 5. The Five Keys to Safer Food manual by WHO offers practical advice on food safety to prevent foodborne illnesses. 6. The Nurturing Care for Early Childhood Development framework focuses on helping children survive and thrive, aiming to transform health and human potential through early interventions. 7. WHO guidelines recommend delayed umbilical cord clamping to improve maternal and infant health and nutrition outcomes. 8. Recommendations for the care of preterm or low birth weight infants are provided by WHO to enhance survival and developmental outcomes. 9. A nutrient and promotion profile model has been developed to support the appropriate marketing of food products for infants and young children aged 6–36 months in the WHO European Region. 10. WHO has issued guidelines for complementary feeding of infants and young children aged 6–23 months, emphasizing the importance of diverse and nutrient-rich diets. 11. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) was formed by identifying experts with technical expertise in complementary feeding and experience in implementing guidelines. Members were selected from academic institutions, Ministries of Health, and non-governmental organizations, ensuring representation from different WHO regions and diverse perspectives. 12. Potential conflicts of interest among GDG members were managed by the steering group in collaboration with the WHO Office of Compliance, Risk Management, and Ethics. All members completed declarations of interest, signed confidentiality forms, and provided their CVs. 13. WHO followed a structured process for developing evidence-based recommendations, including identifying priority questions using the PECO format, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, and formulating recommendations while identifying research gaps. 14. Evidence profile tables were prepared for critical outcomes using the GRADE methodology, assessing the certainty of evidence based on factors like risk of bias, indirectness, inconsistency, imprecision, and publication bias. 15. Meetings were held between 2019 and 2023 to formulate PECO questions, review systematic reviews, develop recommendations, and address research gaps. Decision-making was led by an independent methodologist skilled in WHO's guideline development methodology. 16. A narrative review of literature on complementary feeding since 2003 was commissioned by WHO to inform the development of the guideline. Key questions were formulated on topics such as continued breastfeeding, milk consumption, age of complementary food introduction, dietary diversity, unhealthy foods, and nutrient supplements. 17. WHO commissioned 10 systematic reviews on topics including breastfeeding, milk consumption, complementary food introduction, dietary diversity, fortified foods, unhealthy foods, and responsive feeding. Additional reviews addressed preferences, equity, resource implications, and feasibility. 18. Dietary and food pattern modeling was conducted to analyze how changes in dietary practices could affect nutrient intakes, identifying nutrient gaps and exploring the role of fortified products in addressing these gaps. 19. The modeling used the WHO Optifood system to generate food patterns that meet nutrient reference values. Scenarios were developed to approximate real-world food patterns using data from countries like Bangladesh, Malawi, and Mexico. 20. A systematic review of values and preferences assessed the balance of benefits and harms, resource implications, equity, and acceptability of the recommendations. The findings were appraised using the GRADE-CERQual approach. 21. During meetings, the GDG used the DECIDE framework to facilitate evidence-to-decision deliberations, considering factors like evidence certainty, benefits and harms, values, acceptability, resource implications, equity, and feasibility. 22. The GDG discussed systematic review findings and supplemental evidence, reaching consensus on the direction, strength, and wording of the recommendations.
